hints: Establish a directional sign convention along the line of motion, choosing the initial direction of P as positive.
Particle P rebounds with speed $1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, which means its velocity after collision is $v_P = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Particle Q is initially at rest ($u_Q = 0$).
Apply conservation of linear momentum: $m_P u_P + m_Q u_Q = m_P v_P + m_Q v_Q$, and solve for the speed of Q.
walkthrough:
Apply conservation of linear momentum to the collision between $P$ and $Q$ (taking the initial direction of $P$ as positive, so $u_P = 5$, $u_Q = 0$, $v_P = -1$):
$$m_P u_P + m_Q u_Q = m_P v_P + m_Q v_Q$$
$$0.1(5) + 0.2(0) = 0.1(-1) + 0.2 v_Q$$
$$0.5 = -0.1 + 0.2 v_Q$$

Solve for the velocity of $Q$:
$$0.2 v_Q = 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6$$
$$v_Q = \frac{0.6}{0.2} = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
State the principle of conservation of linear momentum for the direct impact between particles $P$ and $Q$ on the smooth horizontal plane:
$$m_P u_P + m_Q u_Q = m_P v_P + m_Q v_Q$$

Establish a sign convention: let the initial direction of projection of $P$ to the right be positive. List all values:
- Mass of $P$: $m_P = 0.1\text{ kg}$
- Initial velocity of $P$: $u_P = +5\text{ m s}^{-1}$
- Mass of $Q$: $m_Q = 0.2\text{ kg}$
- Initial velocity of $Q$: $u_Q = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (initially at rest)
- Final velocity of $P$: $v_P = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (rebounds to the left)
- Final velocity of $Q$: $v_Q$ (to be found)

Substitute these values into the conservation of momentum equation:
$$(0.1)(5) + (0.2)(0) = (0.1)(-1) + (0.2)v_Q$$
Compute the products:
$$0.5 + 0 = -0.1 + 0.2v_Q$$
$$0.5 = -0.1 + 0.2v_Q$$

Add $0.1$ to both sides:
$$0.5 + 0.1 = 0.2v_Q$$
$$0.6 = 0.2v_Q$$
Divide both sides by $0.2$:
$$v_Q = \frac{0.6}{0.2} = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Thus the speed of $Q$ immediately after the collision is $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

hints: After the first collision, particle P travels to the left with speed $1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (velocity $-1\text{ m s}^{-1}$).
For Q never to collide with P again after hitting R, Q cannot rebound to the left faster than P; therefore its post-collision velocity must satisfy $v_Q' \ge -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Write the conservation of linear momentum for the collision between Q (speed $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$) and R (initially at rest): $m_Q(3) = m_Q v_Q' + m_R V$.
To maximise V, use the minimum allowable velocity for Q, which is $v_Q' = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and solve for V.
walkthrough:
Set up the conservation of linear momentum for the collision between $Q$ ($0.2\text{ kg}$ moving at $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$) and $R$ ($0.5\text{ kg}$ initially at rest):
$$m_Q u_Q + m_R u_R = m_Q v_Q' + m_R V$$
$$0.2(3) + 0.5(0) = 0.2 v_Q' + 0.5 V$$
$$0.6 = 0.2 v_Q' + 0.5 V$$

Apply the condition that $P$ and $Q$ do not collide subsequently. Since $P$ moves to the left at $1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ ($v_P = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$), $Q$ must not catch up with $P$, meaning $v_Q' \ge -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Set $v_Q' = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to achieve the greatest possible value of $V$:
$$0.6 = 0.2(-1) + 0.5 V$$
$$0.6 = -0.2 + 0.5 V$$
$$0.5 V = 0.8 \implies V = \frac{0.8}{0.5} = 1.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough: Analyse the motion of particle $P$ following the first collision: $P$ is moving to the left with constant velocity $v_P = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Particle $Q$ moves to the right with initial velocity $+3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until it collides with $R$ (which is stationary, $u_R = 0$).

State the physical condition preventing a second collision between $P$ and $Q$: after $Q$ collides with $R$, if $Q$ rebounds to the left with speed greater than $1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, it will catch and hit $P$. Therefore, the velocity of $Q$ towards the right must satisfy:
$$v_Q' \ge -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

Apply the conservation of linear momentum to the collision between $Q$ ($m_Q = 0.2\text{ kg}$) and $R$ ($m_R = 0.5\text{ kg}$):
$$m_Q u_Q + m_R u_R = m_Q v_Q' + m_R V$$
Substitute $m_Q = 0.2\text{ kg}$, $u_Q = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $m_R = 0.5\text{ kg}$, and $u_R = 0$:
$$(0.2)(3) + (0.5)(0) = 0.2 v_Q' + 0.5 V$$
$$0.6 = 0.2 v_Q' + 0.5 V$$

Express $V$ in terms of $v_Q'$:
$$0.5 V = 0.6 - 0.2 v_Q'$$
$$V = \frac{0.6 - 0.2 v_Q'}{0.5}$$
To make $V$ as large as possible, we must subtract the smallest possible quantity $0.2 v_Q'$, which occurs when $v_Q'$ takes its lowest permissible value, $v_Q' = -1\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$V_{\text{max}} = \frac{0.6 - 0.2(-1)}{0.5} = \frac{0.6 + 0.2}{0.5} = \frac{0.8}{0.5} = 1.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Thus the greatest possible value of $V$ is $1.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
